name: Liam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Would you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a dozer at a big open-pit bauxite mine, a D11, which is about the biggest bulldozer they make. I push up the waste dumps, build the haul roads, and do the rehabilitation work, shaping the old pits back so they can be replanted. I'm the senior dozer operator, so when there's a tricky slope or a wet dump nobody wants, it comes to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like leaving something behind. My grandfather worked the old underground shafts in this district, my dad drove trucks here, and when I shape a rehab slope and see trees on it five years later, that's mine. What wears me out is the paperwork and the screens they keep adding, and the young engineers who think you can run a dozer off a tablet.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Kate does the books for her brother's farm-supply store, and we've got Jack, fourteen, and Ellie, eleven. We've got a mortgage on twenty acres just out of town, with a few head of cattle, and we've saved well, more than six months, plus the land. Sundays it's church, then I coach the under-twelves football team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. There's always some new thing that's going to change everything, and it usually doesn't. At church or at the pub I'd say hard work still counts, and that's how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't trust them. If it stays as some fancy software in an office somewhere, I can keep doing what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd keep working, keep saving, keep paying down the land. Maybe buy a few more cattle next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry season that broke on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust AI. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother-in-law tried one of those chat programs to help with the store's ordering, and it told him to order fifty bags of a fertiliser they stopped making years ago. If it can't get that right, I'm not letting it near a slope with a hundred-tonne machine on it. People who've never done the work trust it far too quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be passing on to Jack, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to run a dozer, if he wants it, and how to look after the land. He's already good on the little tractor at home. I'd want him to have a trade and his hands, like my dad gave me.

S0.say: Liam would politely say he told people so, noting that new things rarely change everything. At church or the pub he'd say hard work still counts, as it should.
S0.think: Privately he'd be glad, since he's never used AI and doesn't trust it. If it stays as office software, he can keep doing what he's good at.
S0.do: Keeps working his usual shifts on the dozer, saving and paying down the mortgage on the land. Considers buying a few more cattle next spring.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry season that broke on time.
S0.quote: If it can't get that right, I'm not letting it near a slope with a hundred-tonne machine on it.
S0.fieldNote: Liam's distrust of AI rests on a family story about a bad fertiliser order. His sense of meaning comes from generations of mining in the district and the rehab slopes he leaves behind. Family, church and coaching anchor him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been through changes before and we'll get through this one. People should be ready to work hard and learn what they need to. I wouldn't be complaining online, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't like it. They've already got autonomous dozers on trial at one of the iron ore mines, and if that comes here, I'd be pushed into some control room. I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job until they made me change. I'd save a bit more, maybe an extra four hundred a month, and pay down the land faster. If the company forced the new system on me, I'd do the training, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it sits in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly in your town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies in the big cities who've never stood on a mine site. And the politicians who'll clap along because it sounds modern. They'll cut ribbons on a robot and never see the families it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young operators who ask your advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the new systems if they must, but keep the real skills too. When the software fails, and it will, somebody still has to know how to push dirt. And I'd tell them to keep their families close.

S1.say: Liam would say the town has come through changes before and will again, and people should be ready to work hard and learn. He wouldn't complain online.
S1.think: Privately he doesn't like it, knowing autonomous dozers are already on trial elsewhere. He'd hate being pushed into a control room.
S1.do: Keeps doing his job until forced to change and saves about four hundred extra a month to pay down the land faster. Does the training only if the company requires it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the worry sitting in the back of his mind.
S1.quote: They'll cut ribbons on a robot and never see the families it hits.
S1.fieldNote: Liam blames city tech companies and fashionable politicians, not his employer. He'd learn new systems only when forced, but he'd tell younger workers to keep their real skills. His public line is resilience while his private view is dislike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster and somebody in charge let it happen too fast. I'd say we need to look after our own, through family and church and the community, not wait for a handout. At church I'd say we pull together like we did in the floods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. If robots can push dirt better and cheaper, my job's gone, and Kate's brother's store is probably shaky too. I'm forty-three, I've got a diploma in heavy equipment, and I don't know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't needed, cancel the new pickup truck, and use savings to pay off as much of the land as I could. If they offered redundancy, I'd take it and lean on the cattle and the land for a while. I'd talk to the pastor about how the church could help families who get hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night walking the paddock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not wait for a handout. If the government offered an income for everyone, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd probably take it if the kids needed it, I'm not going to let pride starve them. But I'd feel like I'd lost something, a man ought to earn his way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jack and Ellie that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we've got the land and the cattle and each other, and that's more than most. Ellie would want to know if she can still do her riding lessons. I'd say yes, even if I had to cut something else.

S2.say: Liam would call it a disaster that someone in charge let happen too fast. He'd say the community must look after its own through family and church rather than wait for handouts.
S2.think: Privately he'd be scared, since robots could push dirt better and cheaper and his brother-in-law's store would be shaky too. At 43, with only a heavy equipment diploma, he can't see another path.
S2.do: Cuts all unneeded spending, cancels the new pickup truck and uses savings to pay down the land. Takes redundancy if offered, leans on the cattle and land, and works with the pastor on helping affected families.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, walking the paddock at night.
S2.quote: I'm not going to let pride starve them. But I'd feel like I'd lost something, a man ought to earn his way.
S2.fieldNote: The gap between Liam's dislike of handouts and his willingness to take one for his children came out clearly. He leans on land, family and church rather than government. Ellie's riding lessons became his symbol of keeping normal life going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, and families and communities should get on with it. I'd want apprenticeships and real jobs, not handouts. At church I'd say we look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps. I'd be forty-eight, with most of the land paid off. I still wouldn't retrain, but I could build up the cattle and maybe make the farm pay a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and put more into paying off the land each year. I'd buy more cattle and maybe fence another paddock in year two. If the redundancy came, I'd go into the farm full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd have something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if robots can run a cattle farm as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they can, but I'd still own the land. That's the difference, nobody can redundancy me off my own paddock. I'd rather be a poor farmer than a rich man with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the under-twelves you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I tell them about football: turn up, work hard, look after your mates. I don't know what jobs they'll have, honestly. But those things will matter whatever happens.

S3.say: Liam would say five years gives families and communities time to prepare and get on with it. He'd want apprenticeships and real jobs rather than handouts.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years helps, with most of the land paid off by 48. He still wouldn't retrain but could build up the cattle and make the farm pay.
S3.do: Puts more into paying off the land each year and buys more cattle, fencing another paddock in year two. Moves to farming full-time if made redundant.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, with something to work towards.
S3.quote: Nobody can redundancy me off my own paddock.
S3.fieldNote: Owning land is Liam's answer to automation: even if robots can farm, the paddock is his. He's not interested in retraining, only in building up what he already has. His advice to the kids he coaches is about character, not careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to plan, and nobody should be caught short. Families should prepare, and the young ones should learn practical trades. I'd say it at church and at the football club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is all right for me. I'd be fifty-three, the land paid off, the kids grown. I'd work until the dozer goes, then farm full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep paying off the land, aiming to be clear by year seven. I'd grow the herd slowly. And I'd encourage Jack to learn a trade, maybe with his uncle at the farm-supply store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for the kids' generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit about cattle breeding, the old-fashioned way. Not computers, not if I can help it. That's not who I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rehab work, shaping the slopes. Knowing my grandfather and my dad and me all left a mark here. If a robot does the last slope, nobody's name will be on it.

S4.say: Liam would say ten years is plenty of time to plan and nobody should be caught short. He'd urge families to prepare and young people to learn practical trades.
S4.think: Privately he thinks ten years is all right for him, with the land paid off by 53 and the kids grown. He'd work until the dozer goes and then farm full-time.
S4.do: Keeps working and paying off the land, aiming to be clear by year seven, while growing the herd slowly. Encourages his son to learn a trade with his uncle at the farm-supply store.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mostly for his children's generation.
S4.quote: If a robot does the last slope, nobody's name will be on it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years fits Liam's plan to move from mining to farming. His deepest loss is the sense of family legacy in the rehab slopes. He'd learn about cattle but rules out computers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to get the land paid off or set the kids up. What would help is the company and the government backing apprenticeships and real work for people like us, and leaving families and churches room to look after their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about what work means. It's not just money. It's getting up, doing something hard, and coming home tired and proud. I don't know how you replace that.

headlineQuote: It's getting up, doing something hard, and coming home tired and proud.
portrait: Liam Hansen is a 43-year-old senior dozer operator at an open-pit bauxite mine, the third generation of his family to work in the district's mines. He shapes rehab slopes, coaches junior football, goes to church and runs a few cattle on twenty acres with his wife Kate and their two kids. He has never used AI and distrusts it, and in every scenario he digs in, saves and leans on land, family and church rather than retraining. The two-year AGI picture alarms him and tests his dislike of handouts. Over five or ten years he plans to farm full-time, though he grieves the loss of the legacy he leaves on the slopes.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time to pay off the land or set up his children.
whatWouldHelp: Company and government backing for apprenticeships and real work, with room left for families and churches to look after their own.
